_meta.purpose: Cross-engine pricing regression vectors for BTNYC. Each vector pins an exact expected output for a given input, computed from and verified against the live qr.html pricing engine at the time it was added. Run via test_harness/run_vectors.js. A future Python port of the pricing engine (Price Simulator) must also pass every vector here before it is trusted.
_meta.do_not_silently_edit_expected_values: If a vector starts failing after a legitimate pricing-rule change, update the expected value AND note why in a comment here — do not just regenerate the file from whatever the new code produces, or this stops being a regression check.
_meta.design_principle: This file is NOT a catalog of hardcoded scenarios and is never read by btnyc.json, qr.html, or btnyc.py at runtime — it's an external, offline regression suite, isolated from the live SSOT. Vectors that exercise a `dynKey`/`formulaId` (the dynamic_services + pricing_formulas path) use arbitrary sample qty/answer values purely to pin ONE concrete input/output pair for a GENERIC formula that already handles any qty or item combination — they are proof the generic math works, never a proposal to hardcode that specific qty/item as its own named service. The entire point of dynamic_services + pricing_formulas is that nobody ever has to author a discrete catalog entry per unique customer request.

vectors.description: 5 subway tiles, no grout repair, no water damage, no high ceiling, no disposal — the 'easy' tile case. Distinguishes from tile_floor_with_grout below: same quantity, materially different job.

5 floor tiles requiring grout repair — same quantity as tile_subway_no_grout, but grouting adds $25 + 20min per the formula's grout_penalty. This is the exact nuance flagged as critical: identical qty, different job.
Stacked penalties — water damage AND high ceiling both apply on top of base tile work. Verifies penalties accumulate rather than override each other.

Sample input proving furniture_repair_formula's GENERIC per-unit scaling math (qty=5 and 'Broken piece' are arbitrary sample values here, not a hardcoded scenario — the formula itself takes any qty and any issue_type_fees key identically; this vector just needs ONE concrete input/output pair to pin as a regression check). Verifies the issue fee is charged ONCE regardless of qty (not multiplied by qty) while minutes scale per ADDITIONAL unit via per_unit_minutes — i.e. N small repairs of the same issue type are priced as one visit handling N items, never as N separate full visits. This is the dynamic_services formula path — there is no and should never be a named/catalog service for any specific quantity or furniture-item combination; the formula is what makes hardcoding every possible combination unnecessary.
Single drawer that sticks — baseline single-unit furniture repair, no per-unit scaling involved (qty=1).

answers.issue: Drawer that sticks or falls out

vectors.description: Drywall patch, 10 sqft, texture match requested.
PAX wardrobe: 2 cabinet frames, 4 hinge doors, 0 sliding, 3 interior items. Verifies the coefficient-based hour calculation (not a flat per-unit fee like the other formulas).

3 separate end-table assemblies at 20 min each, summed before the 1-hour minimum is applied — must land at exactly 1hr/$65, NOT 3x 1hr minimums ($195). This is the 'don't penalize multiple small assemblies' rule.
A single 20-minute assembly still gets the 1-hour minimum (no on-site visit is worth less than that), confirming the floor applies even to one small job.

Regression anchor for the v9.2 baseline-timing fix. dishwasher_repair is hourly-priced with a curated 70-390min range (wide, because dishwasher repair genuinely varies a lot) and a 'specialized' complexity tier ($110/hr) — this is the named service with the largest verified divergence between the old flat-45min placeholder and the curated 230min midpoint ($193 old vs $422 correct, +$229). Pinned here so this regression can never silently reappear. (Note: an earlier manual calculation of this vector incorrectly assumed the 'skilled' $85 rate and produced $532 — corrected here after running the actual byte-for-byte old code against the actual current code. See CHANGELOG_v9.2.md for the full corrected divergence table across all 10 affected services, including two services that went DOWN in price, not up.)

Regression anchor confirming flat_rate services are correctly UNAFFECTED by the baseline-timing fix — toilet_install ignores total_minutes entirely for billing (flat base_price + extraFee, no hourly multiplication). Included specifically because this service was incorrectly used as the divergence example in an earlier (wrong) verification pass — pinned here so that mistake can't recur unnoticed.

Second hourly divergence anchor ($184 old vs $358 correct). Also documents a real engine behavior worth knowing: this service is tagged operational_metrics.complexity_tier='skilled', but its curated 120-140min duration falls in the 'specialized' band (91+ min) per global_rules.complexity_tiers — deriveComplexityTier takes the HIGHER-ranked of the duration-derived tier and the tagged exactTier, so this correctly bills at the $110 specialized rate, not the $85 skilled rate the tag alone would suggest. Not a bug: a job whose curated time clearly runs long shouldn't get the cheap rate just because of an early, possibly-stale operational_metrics tag.

IMPORTANT: this is one of TWO services (the other is furniture_repair_hourly) where the v9.2 baseline-timing fix DECREASED the quoted price ($114 old -> $71 correct, -$43), not increased it. Its curated range (40-60min, midpoint 50) is genuinely shorter than the old flat-45-plus-rounding-quirk happened to produce. This vector exists specifically so a future 'fix' attempt that assumes the correction should always raise prices doesn't break this service trying to push it back up.

The second of the two services that decreased after the fix ($114 old vs $113 correct, -$1 — effectively a wash, but still technically a decrease, included for completeness alongside furniture_disassembly_for_moving).

v9.5 FIX (supersedes the old escalation_wall_mount_drywall_routine anchor — see CHANGELOG/BACKLOG_CONSOLIDATED.md item A for the full story). The OLD expected value (routine/$109) relied on a real, severe, systemic bug: computeUnifiedQuote's baseMinutes computation never read dynDef's own real, curated default_estimate.total_minutes (60-80 min for wall_mounting+Mount) — it fell through to a bare 45-minute fallback that happened to land EXACTLY on the routine/skilled tier boundary by coincidence. With the real, curated duration now correctly used (midpoint 70 min), this dynamic service genuinely, honestly belongs in the skilled tier regardless of wall_type — confirmed via direct hand-calculation against the real data, not just code output. If this vector ever regresses to routine/$109, the baseMinutes-from-dynDef fix has been lost again.

v9.5 FIX (supersedes the old escalation_wall_mount_brick_skilled anchor). Same real-duration fix as the drywall vector above — now BOTH wall types genuinely land in 'skilled' on duration alone, so the tier itself no longer distinguishes them. This vector instead verifies the thing that's still genuinely true and still worth protecting: wall_type's own answer-level effects (Brick: +$25 fee, +20 min) correctly stack ON TOP of the shared real duration baseline, so brick still costs MORE than drywall ($213 vs $159, a real +$54 difference) even though both now share the same complexity tier. If this vector's price ever equals the drywall vector's price, the answer-level fee/minutes plumbing has broken.
